deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Gauss's lemniscatic material. P is the entire numerator function in sl x = P(x)/Q(x). In modern terms it is the Weierstrass sigma function of the square lattice ϖZ[i], with g2=4 and g3=0. Here ϖ = 2∫_0^1 dt/√(1−t⁴) = Γ(1/4)²/(2√(2π)) ≈ 2.62206.

(1) Definition. Gauss writes Pφ = φ − φ⁵/60 + &c. This is the series Gauss elsewhere gives as M(x) = x − 2x⁵/5! − 36x⁹/9! − … . Since 2/5! = 1/60, P = M. It agrees with σ(u) = u − g2u⁵/240 − … for g2 = 4.

(2) Theta expansion. Put z = a+bi and q = e^{−π}. Gauss states
P(zϖ)·e^{−πz²/2} = √(π/(ϖ√2))·(2e^{−π/4} sin πz − 2e^{−9π/4} sin 3πz + …).
That is P' = √(π/(ϖ√2))·θ1(πz, e^{−π}). The prefactor is defined by P' = P/e^{(½a² + abi − ½b²)π}, and ½a² + abi − ½b² is exactly z²/2.
Check (mine): for the lattice with 2ω1 = ϖ, 2ω3 = iϖ, the Legendre relation with η3 = −iη1 gives η1 = π/(2ϖ). Hence the factor exp(η1u²/(2ω1)) becomes e^{πz²/2} at u = zϖ. Also θ1'(0) = θ2θ3θ4 = 2^{−1/2}θ3³ with θ3² = √2ϖ/π, so θ1'(0) = 2^{1/4}(ϖ/π)^{3/2}. Then (2ω1/π)/θ1'(0) = √(π/(ϖ√2)). So Gauss's constant is exactly right.

(3) Second normalization. P'' = P/e^{(½a² − abi + ½b²)π}. Gauss notes P'' = P'/e^{(b² − 2abi)π}; the exponent difference is indeed b² − 2abi. So P'' = P(zϖ)·e^{−π|z|²/2}·e^{πabi}, and |P''| = |P(zϖ)|e^{−π|z|²/2}. This is the standard lattice-normalized modulus of sigma.

(4) Exponential form. With π understood, 2 sin kπz = (e^{(aki−bk)π} − e^{(−aki+bk)π})/i. So each term is ±e^{−k²π/4}(e^{(aki−bk)π} − e^{(−aki+bk)π})/i. Splitting the two exponentials lets k run over all odd integers, positive and negative ('k alle posit. und neg. ungeraden'), with sign (−1)^{(k−1)/2}. Thus
P' = √(π/(ϖ√2))·(1/i)·Σ_{k odd} (−1)^{(k−1)/2} e^{π(−k²/4 + ikz)}.

(5) Result. Multiplying by e^{−(b²−2abi)π}:
P'' = √(π/(ϖ√2))·(1/i)·Σ_{k odd} ± e^{(−k²/4 − bk + aki − b² + 2abi)π},
with π and the sign tacitly understood. Implicit next step (mine): the exponent equals π[−(k/2+b)² + 2ai(k/2+b)]. So P'' is a Gaussian sum in b + k/2. Under b → b+1 it changes only by sign (k → k−2). So |P''| is periodic and bounded, presumably preparing a symmetric (a↔b) treatment or a Poisson/Jacobi-type transformation. The page breaks off here.
errors: Second term of the series: exponent written e^{−9/4} without π; it should be e^{−9π/4} (the first term correctly has e^{−π/4}). Slip of the pen.

In the line ±e^{−kk/4}·e^{aki−bk} − e^{−aki+bk} and in the final P'' formula, the factor π is omitted from all exponents. Brackets around the difference are also missing, and the alternating sign (−1)^{(k−1)/2} is left implicit as ±/Σ. With these understood, the formulas are correct.
The factor 1/2 between 2 sin and (e^{…} − e^{…})/i is absorbed correctly, since the coefficient 2 cancels.

results.what: P(φ) = φ − φ⁵/60 + … as the numerator of the lemniscatic sine (sl = P/Q)
results.modern_name: Weierstrass sigma function for the square lattice ϖZ[i] (g2=4, g3=0)
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass (1860s–1880s); Gauss's lemniscatic M,N functions (c.1797–1800) published in Werke III

results.what: P(zϖ) = e^{πz²/2}·√(π/(ϖ√2))·Σ(−1)^n 2e^{−π(n+1/2)²} sin((2n+1)πz), with the exact constant
results.modern_name: sigma function as Gaussian factor times Jacobi θ1 (σ(u) = (2ω/π)e^{ηu²/2ω}θ1(πu/2ω)/θ1'(0)), lemniscatic case q=e^{−π}
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (Fundamenta Nova 1829) and Weierstrass; Gauss's lemniscatic theta formulas known from Werke III

results.what: Normalization P'' = P(zϖ)e^{−π|z|²/2}e^{πiab}, written as a bilateral sum over odd k with exponent −π(k/2+b)² + 2πia(k/2+b)
results.modern_name: lattice-invariant normalized modulus |σ(u)|e^{−π|u|²/(2A)} (Klein form / Néron-type normalization); theta series in Gaussian form
results.usually_credited_to: standard in 19th–20th c. theory of theta functions (Klein, Hermite; later Néron)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's theta expansion of the lemniscatic numerator function, including the constant, is documented in his published Nachlass (Werke III). The rewriting with the factor e^{−π|z|²/2} as a bilateral Gaussian sum is a natural manipulation, though it anticipates the modern normalized-sigma viewpoint. It is a correct and tidy unpublished detail, not a new theorem.
